speechtext: On the Orders of the Day:

In
the course of my speech on Tuesday evening I was asked by the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) whether certain figures that I had presented as the average wages earned in Canada by those employed in the manufacturing industries included salaries. On the spur of the moment I replied in the affirmative, but on going over the figures again I find that I should have answered in the negative. I want to take this opportunity of correcting that statement in fairness to all concerned.

speechtext: On the Orders of the Day:

maintopic: REPORTED STATEMENT OF HON. MR. BOIVIN
speechtext: I beg to call the attention of the Minister of Customs and Excise (Mr. Boivin) to a report which appeared in this morning's Citizen, as well as in other newspapers, of a speech which is alleged to have been made by him in Montreal yesterday. The minister, according to the report, made the statement that he did not think that the people wanted an election, and he proceeded to say that all that had been discussed at Ottawa was whether a Governor General from England would decide or whether the people should choose. May I ask the minister whether that report is correct or not? If it is, then the statement would seem to me to be a most injudicious one.

speakeroldname: Hon. G. H. BOIVIN (Minister of Customs and Excise):
maintopic: REPORTED STATEMENT OF HON. MR. BOIVIN
speechtext:
I am glad to have the opportunity of replying to the question asked by my hon. friend. It is true that I spoke in Montreal last night before the members of the Young Men's Association at the Montreal Reform Club. I hope that those who do me the honour of reading the press reports of my speech will not attribute the misleading headings to myself. The headings as everyone knows are the work of the editors of the respective newspapers in which the report appears and were not inspired by me. As regards the specific statement that has been brought to my attention by the hon. gentle-

The Address-Mr. Doucet
man, the exact translation of the words which I used in the French language would be as follows: The question that has been decided at Ottawa was whether or not the leader of the government should be chosen by the people of Canada through their elected representatives or by His Excellency the Governor General upon the advice of one who was described by the opposition as a defeated Prime Minister. I am sorry that the words "His Excellency " were not used in the translation; they should have been there, as also the words "upon the advice of one who was described by the opposition as a defeated Prime Minister."

maintopic: REPORTED STATEMENT OF HON. MR. BOIVIN

member to deny having used the phrase, "Governor General from England"?

maintopic: REPORTED STATEMENT OF HON. MR. BOIVIN

The House resumed from Wednesday, January 20, consideration of the motion of Mr. J. C. Elliott for an Address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his Speech at the opening of the session, and the proposed amendment thereto of Right Hon. Arthur Meighen.
Mr. ALEXANDER J. DOUOET (Kent, N.B.): Mr. Speaker, when the House rose last evening I was discussing the platforms upon which the last election was contested throughout the Dominion. I had reached that stage where I had demonstrated-conclusively, I believe-that in the Maritime provinces, instead of being elected as a Maritime group ready to oppose our right hon. leader (Mr. Meighen) we were returned on the policies of
a protective tariff and consideration of our transportation problem as dealt with by my right hon. leader in his speech of June 2 last.
Now I come to the province of Ontario. Yesterday afternoon the hon. member for South Perth (Mr. Sanderson) said that the tariff was the real issue in that province. But I ask this House, what was the issue in the seventeen Ontario ridings where the government had no candidates? Certainly it was a most extraordinary thing that in the last election 31 out of the 245 seats were not contested by the government; in other words, in 12i per cent of the federal seats, or one-eight of the whole representation, the government could not find candidates willing to sacrifice themselves to their political convictions. If the tariff was the real issue in the province of Ontario, unquestionably the great majority of the electors in that province decided emphatically in favour of the programme offered by my right hon. leader.
Next let me deal with the provinces of Manitoba and Saskatchewan. The hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Howden) said that the issue in the west was transportation. But in Manitoba I find the government failed to contest six constituencies. In Saskatchewan they allowed two to go by default-Long Lake and Qu'Appelle. I think we see before us this afternoon the reason why Long Lake was not contested by the government. In Alberta the government also allowed two seats to go by default. If transportation was the primary question in the prairie provinces, then most assuredly the Conservative vote in the last election compared with that polled in 1921 shows that the people out there have faith in the proposition put forward by our party to make it possible to transport the products of the east and the west to the central provinces, and if need be, let the whole country shoulder the burden.
Now I come to a discussion of the campaign in the old province of Quebec. This is the more important, Sir, because 60 per cent of the hon. members sitting on your right were returned by that province; that is, out of an available 99 votes, 60 are from Quebec. In that I am not including the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa). I purpose to show that some of the propaganda used and some of the speeches delivered in that province on behalf of the government were entirely aside from the real issue-the tariff. Throughout the campaign in that province our friends discussed in the majority of the constituencies every other issue but the tariff, and to confirm my statement I need quote only from Le Soleil, the chief Liberal organ in the province
The Address-Mr. Doucet

of Quebec. In its editorial columns of October 15 last I find the following:
A bas T imperial! isme!
Nos adversaires ont cherch6 a distraire 1'esprdt du peuple de la question vitale de Ja presente campagne, en aveuglant l'electorat de chiffres et de th6ories pro-tectionnistes. La question supreme, celle qui domine toutes les autres, c'est Timp^rialisme.
I do not want to vouch for the translation, but to me that quotation would read something like this:
Down With Imperialism
Our opponents have tried to divert public opinion from the important question of this campaign by blindfolding the electors with statistics and protectionist theories. The supreme question, that which overshadows all others, is imperialism.
Now, Sir, I think I shall be able to establish by further quotations that in some sections of that good province the campaign was carried on as a campaign of hatred and prejudice by the chief Liberal organs of the province, by some of the most outstanding' speakers of the province, and even by some of the ministers of the crown.

Will the
hon. member allow me to ask him a question? In order to make it clear to the House, would he tell us what were the views of the leader who had charge of the opposition campaign in the province of Quebec?
With reference to Imperialism.
Of Canada.

I have no hesitation in
using that phrase-the grand old man of Canada-speaking August 19, 1914, in this House said:
The gravity of the occasion which has called us together makes it incumbent upon us even to disregard the formalities and conventionailities which in ordinary times the rules of the House, written and unwritten, enjoin as a wise safeguard against precipitate action, but which, on such an occasion as this, might impede us in dealing with the momentous question before us. This session has been called for the purpose of giving the authority of parliament and the sanction of law to such measures as have already been taken by the government, and any further measures that may be needed, to insure the defence of Canada and to give what aid may be in our power to the Mother Country in the stupendous struggle which now confronts her. Speaking for those who sit around me-
He occupied the seat which my right hon. leader occupies at the moment.
-speaking for the wide constituencies which we represent in this House, I hasten to say that to all these measures we are prepared to give immediate assent.
Not only in the beginning, but later on during the debate he used these words:
But to-day the spectre of civil ifrar has vanished from Ireland; all Irishmen are united, ready to fight for king and country. The volunteers of the north and the volunteers of the south, forgetting their past differences, stand shoulder to shoulder ready to shed thedr blood for the common cause. And, Sir, may I not say that the hope is not vain that in that baptism of blood may be washed away, and forever washed away, the distrust of one another which has been the curse of Ireland in ages past.
But it is not only in Ireland that you find this union of hearts. In the two other united kingdoms the voice of faction has been silenced. Even those who on principle do not believe in war admit that this was a just war and that it had to be fought. That union of hearts which exists in the United Kingdom exists also in Canada, in Australia, in New Zealand. Yea, even in South Africa-South Africa, rent by war less than twenty years ago, but now united under the blessing of British institutions, with all, British and Dutch together, standing ready to shed their blood for the common cause. Sir, there is in this the inspiration and the hope that from this painful war the British Empire may emerge with a new bond of union, the pride of ail its citizens, and a living light to afll other nations.
That bond, sir, you cannot maintain, that tie you cannot cement, by political campaigns begun and carried on in such a spirit as the editorial I have just read to the House exemplifies.

Will my hon. friend state
whether, when the words he has just quoted were pronounced, conscription existed in Ireland, Australia or New Zealand, or in any other British dominion except Canada?

It did not exist in
Canada.

I am not a student of
history, and I do not happen to have under my hand at the present moment the information which my hon. friend the Solicitor General (Mr. Cannon) seeks, but what I do know is this, that in 1898, there were no provisions in the Militia Act whereby soldiers could be sent from Canada to participate in a war overseas. I know this further, that the party of the hon. gentleman seem to blame the Tories of this Dominion for everything done since confederation in connection with Canada's part in overseas wars, but I want to point out that it was the amendments that were made to the Militia Act in 1908 by my hon. friend's own party that made it possible for Canadians to be sent overseas to fight.
The leader of the Liberal party of that day expressed his views on the question of Canada's participation in the war on the floor of this House, and those of you who wish to read it will find reported on page seven of Le Soleil of Friday, September 25, 1914, that speaking before a convention of Methodists in Ottawa at that time, Sir Wilfrid Laurier used these words:
Adressant la parole a un convention de methodistes, k Ottawa, sir Wilfrid Laurier dedlara, en parlant de la guerre, que "nous devions etre fiers de ne pas etre les agresseurs dans le present conflit. Nous devons etre fiers," dit-il "malgre toute la repugnance que nous avons pour la guerre, de participer a cette guerre pares que *nous combattons pour la cause de la justice et de la sincerity. L'histoire fait voir que '.orsque 1'empire britannique entra en guerre, c'Stait parce que la paix ne pouvait pas etre honorablement maintenue. Notre devoir en Canada est d'aider la mere patrie jusqu'k la contribution de notre dernier dollar, et la participation de notre dernier soldat, si necessaire.
Nearly all the members of this House must have read the statement published in the papers, and repeated by hon. members opposite, that the right hon. leader of the opposition was the man who first said that this country was in the war to the last man and the last dollar. Now, I will translate the passage I have just quoted from Le Soleil of September 25, 1914:
Addressing a Methodist convention Held in Ottawa, Sir W'ilfrid Laurier said, speaking of the war: "We ought to be proud not to be the aggressors in the present conflict. We ought to be proud in spite of our disgust for war to participate in the present struggle, because we are fighting for the cause of justice and sincerity. History teaches us that when the British Empire took part in a war it was because peace could not honourably be maintained. It is our duty as Canadians to aid the Mother Country, even by contributing our last dollar and our last man, if necessary.
The Address-Mr. Doucet

Those were the words of the then great chieftain of the Liberal party, and we have to-day unmistakable evidence-evidence that cannot be contradicted-that those who follow him in this country, and who pretend to recall the spirit of that grand old man to the electors of their province, have at the same time practically accused him of disloyalty by pretending that he was opposed to any participation by Canada in empire ware, and they lay the whole blame for Canada's participation in the war, if blame it be, on the leader of the opposition.

Will my hon. friend say
whether he took any part in the election in the province of Quebec in 1925?

What has that to do with
it?
I am addressing my hon. friend from Kent, N.B. (Mr. Doucet).
The question is irrelevant.

Never mind the interruptions; I rather invite them. Once you get under a man's skin, he generally squirms. I was not hesitating to give my hon. friend the Solicitor General an answer; I only waited for him to resume his seat. I took no part in the general elections in Quebec in 1925, but I did take part in the by-election in the county of Rimouski in 1924, and I want to say this for the hon. member for Rimouski (Sir Eugene Fiset), that, in his own by-election of 1924, I do not believe he was guilty of using any of the stuff that was used in the last general election.
SIR EUGENE FISET: Will you kindly tell me if in that by-election of 1924 you and your-
Order.

Order. I must remind
hon. members, first, that interruptions can take place only with the consent of the hon. gentleman who has the floor; secondly, that when an hon. member addresses the House he must address himself to the Chair. Otherwise, we cannot have orderly debate.

As a general rule I have
no objection whatever to interruptions.
You have quoted from Le Soleil and have drawn conclusions-
Order.
I would ask hon. gentlemen not to interrupt. It is not conducive to order.

I have so far been allowed to quote only from Le Soleil. I can, however, assure hon. gentlemen opposite that if they will give me time, and I assure them they will lose nothing by waiting, I shall quote from other sources. I did not know that hon. gentlemen opposite had so much "repugnance" to Le Soleil. I qualified my assertions at the outset by stating that this had occurred in some of the counties of the province of Quebec, but I think before I take my seat I shall be able to show that this sort of campaign was carried on in most of the counties in Quebec during the last election, and not only in the province of Quebec, for Le Soleil was distributed to every house in my own constituency, and house to house canvasses were made and the people told that if Doucet was elected we would have a war with Turkey within thirty days.
In that same editorial from which I have just quoted I find this:
Huit annees nous separent de l'nnnSe terrible, eelle de la conscription. C'est beaucoup dans la vie d'un in-dividu. En huit ans, des memoires, surtout parmi lea peisonnes a peine arrivees 4 la majorite, ont le temps d'oublier. Mais la Providence, qui veille sur lea des-tinees de3 peoples, a suscite, au cours de ces dernieres annees, un incident qui a ravive le souvenir de la grande tragedie de 1917 et reveille les justes coleres. Bile a rendu 4 la question de participation forcee toute son actuality.
I translate as follows for the edification of hon. members:
Eight years stand between us and the terrible year, the conscription year. This is quite a stretch in the life of an individual. In the course of eight years, memories fade, particularly in the case of persons who barely reached their majority. But Providence which keeps a watchful vigil on the destinies of people, has brought forth in the course of the last few years an incident which revived the memory of the great tragedy of 1917 and aroused righteous anger. It has restored to the question of compulsory participation its fullest actuality.
Further on the same editorial says:
Ready, aye ready we are!
Hear, hear.

My hon. friend the Solicitor
General says "Ecoutez, ecoutez."

Sans doute.
Ready, Aye, ready we are! Paroles providenfciella* qui sauveront le Canada du gouffre imperialiste 1 Grftce k elles, 1 indignation populaire s'abattera de nouveau sur le faeatique qui les pronongat.
Ready, Aye, ready, we are! Providential words which will save Canada from the chasm of imperialism. Thanks to them, popular indignation will once more fall upon the fanatic who uttered them.
And it concludes:
Done, Arthur Meighen met le Canada en danger.
Or:
Therefore, Arthur Meighen puts Canada in danger.

The Address-Mr. Doucet
That is part of the campaign literature which was distributed throughout Quebec and parts of New Brunswick during the campaign, and yet certain hon. members from the province of Quebec and ministers of the crown claim the campaign was fought on the issue of protection.
Oh, oh.

The hon. gentleman did
not make clear his assertion-
Order.

I simply want to ask my
hon. friend a question.
Ask it and do not make a speech.

The hon. gentleman has not made good his assertion that it was claimed that if Mr. Meighen were returned to power war would be declared with Turkey at once. From what paper or what editorial can he quote anything of the kind?

I did not make that assertion and Hansard will bear me out but the insinuations throughout the editorial would certainly lead one to believe it. What I stated was that in my constituency eanvassers, on behalf of the Liberal government, went from house to house and declared that if Doucet were elected we would have war with Turkey immediately. Until that time I had no knowledge of my importance as a factor in imperial politics. To show that this editorial "down with imperialism" was found to be very acceptable to its subscribers and was thought to be doing good work throughout the province it was reprinted in Le Soleil of October 28, 1925, just on the eve of the election. We must conclude that those responsible for it thought it had produced an effect and that by reprinting it the editorial might do better work yet. I quote from the editorial in question the following:
En cas de conflit, on salt ce que ferait Arthur Meighen. II recommencerait les orgies de 1914 et pous-serait la logique de son fanatisme jusqu'k la conscription et a l'abolition presque complete de notre souve* rained parlementaire.
Est-ce que le peuple se laissera entminer h tel point en de vaines considerations protectionnistes qu il en oublie la grande question nationale par excellence: l'autonomie du Canada et la lutte a un impSrialisme desastreux.
I translate this as follows:
In the event of a conflict we know what Arthur Meighen would do. He would repeat the orgies of 1914, and would carry the logic of his fanaticism to conscription and to the almost complete abolition of our parliamentary sovereignty. Will the people allow themselves to be led to such a degree by vain protectionist considerations, that they will forget the 14011-20
great and outstanding national issue of the autonomy of Canada and the fight against a disastrous imperialism?
Apparently the fiscal policy of Canada, party programmes, and so on were not the questions at issue. The real issue was autonomy for Canada and a fight against imperialism. The editorial concludes as follows:
L'eleetorat devra bientot choisir en ces deux chefs.
II lui appartient de decider s'il consent a risquer de renouveler I'aventure de 1914 a 1918.
Translated it reads:
The electorate must soon make a choice between these two leaders. It behooves it to decide whether it is willing to risk a renewal of the adventure of 1914 to 1918.
Now, Mr. Speaker, sometimes cartoons are very instructive, and when one has not very much to do they serve to while the time away.
I have a cartoon here issued by Le Soleil on October 24, 1925. In the French inscription Mr. Meighen is made to say:
Jusqu'au dernier sou, jusqu'au dernier homme pour l'empire.
The last dollar, the last man for the empire.
You have here the leader of the opposition and standing in the background Mr. Gauthier and Mr. Patenaude. On the other side you have Mackenzie King in the foreground and close by I see the smiling countenances of my hon. friends Messrs. Lapointe, Cardin and Cannon. Mr. King says:
Pas un sou ne sera depense, pas un homme ne sera mobilise pour l'empire.
The translation of the French inscription attached to the cartoon in which Mr. King and his colleagues appear is:
Not a dollar will be expended, not a man will be mobilized for the empire.
That is King's idea?

Yes, that is King's idea.
This cartoon was distributed through the medium of the chief Liberal organ of the province of Quebec. One hon. gentleman from the province of Quebec felt somewhat cross because I included the representatives of the entire province in this category. I made it clear, however, that what I was giving were quotations from some of the Liberal organs. I have now to give a quotation from a speech made by the Solicitor General at Trois Rivieres.
I never spoke there.
Take it back.
Read the quotation and let us see where he did speak.

I shall quote from Le
Soleil of October 15. The despatch is dated

The Address-Mr. Doucet

"Trois Rivieres, October 15, from our special correspondent." I see the meeting was at Grand'Mere. That does not matter very much; it could not have been very far from Trois Rivieres when a correspondent sent his information from that town. The despatch says that the meeting was held at the city hall of Grand'Mere which was packed! to the doors. I do not think the Solicitor General will deny that fact.
I spoke at Grandi'Mere. I did not speak at Three Rivers.

This report says speaking of my right hon. leader:
II est l'auiteur de la loi de conscription, ill est l'au-teur de ces ordre3 en conseil pour autoriser la poflice k venir chercher les consents dans vos campagnes et meme k se servir de chiens policiere. Etes-vous en fa-veur de 1'avoir?
The English translation of that statement is:
He is the author of the Conscription Act, he is the author of the orders in council authorizing the police to hunt the conscripts in our rural districts and even to make use of police dogs. Do you favor his election?
Low tariff!

If that were printed by
some paper not recognized as the chief organ of the party, or spoken at some meeting by some would-be political campaigners who have no responsibility in this House, or who may never acquire that responsibility, we might ignore it, but that comes from a minister of the crown-a member of the government. He was speaking to a meeting of electors in the constituency of Three Rivers-St. Maurice.
In order to shorten my hon. friend's remarks, I may tell him that I do not take back one word of what I said.
Where does that come in the tariff?
I will show my hon. friend later.

The Solicitor General (Mr. Cannon) will have ample opportunity to show wherein he stands and how he can connect that with one of the planks of the platform of 1919 which I have before me and which reads:
Resolution on National Unity
Recognizing that the crown of Six Wilfrid Laurier's life work and the dearest wish of his heart was the establishment of racial concord and national unity throughout the Dominion, the Liberal party of Canada in national convention assembled emphatically condemns all attempts to create racial discord and national disunion and would hold up as a lasting example to the Canadian people the inspiring ideal of that great Canadian-a united Canada in which all Canadian!
fMr. Doucet.]
shall be on an equal footing, all working together in harmony and concord for the upbuilding and aggrandizement of their common country.
Those are very eloquent words, and I wonder not that they are applauded by hon. members opposite, but, Sir, I say that the old adage, "Example is better than precept" should be applied. And rather than applaud the reading of the paragraph, they should practice what they preach.
Now, Sir, the same minister of the crown, speaking at St-Malachie, is reported as follows:
L'honorable M. Cannon fait alors remarquer que si la guerre est finie elle peut recommencer. II im-porte done de prtivenir les coups et de ne pas mettre k la tete du gouvernement un homme 'toujours pret k lancer le Canada dans un nouveau conflit comme si le grand derangement de 1914-18 n'avait pas fait couler assez de larmes dans nos foyers, (appl.)
Translated:
The Hon. Mr. Cannon observed that if the war was over it might break out again.
That is the low tariff campaign.
It is therefore imperative that a recurrence of such happenings be prevented by not placing at the head of the government a man who is ever ready to throw Canada into a fresh conflict as if the great disturbance of 1914-1918 had not caused enough tears to be shed in our homes. (Applause.)
Those were the words of the Solicitor General himself.
Promoting unity.

Promoting unity-national unity. It would be interesting to have just at this moment a copy of the Toronto Globe of the following morning-I was going to say the morning after the night before-the morning following the evening on which my hon.
friend spoke in Toronto, and to
4 p.m. compare those words with the words used! at GrandtMere and the other places I have mentioned. But he is not the only one, there are others in the same class and in the same boat. They often say they are misquoted, but the Hon. L. A. Tasehereau, Premier of the province of Quebec-
He is not here.

No, he is not here, but
he spoke of those who were not present when he was speaking at Chateau Richer, and L'Evenement of October 34, 1925, reports him as saying:
"Combien de jeunes gens", dit 1'honorable M. Tasehereau, "sont alors venus nous demander de les faire exempter du service militaire! Mais la loi Borden-Meighen 6tait inexorable. II fallait partir pour Valcartier. Soixante mille des notres sont tomb^s sur lo champ de bataille europ^en."

The Address-Mr. Doucet
The translation reads:
"How many young men", said the Hon. Mr. Tas-chereau, "came to us and asked us to have them exempted from military service? But the Meighen-Borden law was inexorable. They had to leave for Valcartier. Sixty thousand of our sons fell on European battle-fields."
If that be true, what would have been the situation if the law o.f 1908 had been applied without any provision for exemption? The most that can fee charged against those who were responsible for the administration of affairs in those days was that they applied compulsory service; but they took the means by which those who had the right to be exempted could be exempted, and not drawn by lot, as they would have been under the law of 1908, prepared by the Liberal government. I admit, Sir, that that was correct, and my hon. friend the member for Rimouski (Sir Eugene Fiset) who was Deputy Minister of Militia at the time, and who undoubtedly had charge of the administration of that part of the act, knows full well that it was true.

The hon. member
knows that I did not administer that act.

My hon. friend will have
an opportunity to correct any statements in regard to which he thinks I may be wrong, but I should like to proceed now without interruption. But there were others too. The hon. member for Quebec West (Mr. Parent), who is not altogether a [DOT] stranger to that Liberal organ from which I have been quoting all afternoon, held a meeting at St. Augustine in his constituency, and although he himself did not make any statements out of the ordinary,-at least no such statements were attributed to him in that paper-he had with him a young man by the name of Jean Marie Fortin of Le Soleil, who said:
On ne peut oublier des gens qui nous ont claqufl dans le dos, mais s'il en est parmi vous qui veulent encore des jobs h $1.10 par jour, pour s'en aller pour-rir dans les tranchees ils n'ont qu 'h voter pour Meighen et Patenaude.
We cannot forget those who formerly knifed us in the back, but if there are any who are still looking for jobs at a dollar ten a day to go an rot in the trenches all they have to do is to vote for Meighen and Patenaude.
The reporter Says that there was applause and I suppose that the hon. member for Quebec West applauded with the rest of them. I have here a little pamphlet, the sort of thing we call a dodger in business, and although it is one of the requirements of our election law that the name of the printer shall appear at the bottom of every pamphlet or piece of printed matter circulated in connection with any election, I notice that this 14011-20J
particular pamphlet does not comply with the act in this respect. It declares:
Un vote pour Davidson est un vote assur6 pour Meighen, le pere de la Conscription.
Si vous voulez que vos fils aillent & la guerre, votez pour Davidson.
A vote for Davidson is a sure vote for Meighen the father of conscription. If you want your sons to go to war vote for Davidson.
There was another member of the provincial government of Quebec who took part in that campaign, the Hon. J. E. Perreault, Minister of Mines and Colonization, who spoke at Victoriaville in the county of Drummond-Arthabaska. This gentleman, who has not so far denied it, is reported as having said:
Vous savez comme moi que M. Meighen est l'auteur de toutes les iniquit^s du regime bleu, qu'il est II'auteur de la fameuse loi de conscription et qu'il s'en vante. Vous vous rappedez, jeunes gems de Victoriaville, les tristes jours que nous avons v6cu pendant que Meighen etait au pouvoir. Vous vous rap.pelez que merae apres la guerre, alors que tous les pays avaient pardonnS aux conscrits qui ne s'6taient pas rapport^s, M. Meighen les pourchassait quand meme et faisait remplir par ses agents da prison d'Arthabaska.
You are aware as well as I am that Mr. Meighen is the author of all the iniquities of the bleu regime- that is, the Tory regime. He is the author of the famous Conscription Act and he boasts about it. Young men of Victoriaville, you recall the sad days we lived through while Meighen was m power. You recall that even after the war, when all countries had pardoned the draftees who had not reported for military service, Mr. Meighen still kept on their trail and had his agents filling the Arthabaska jail.
What paper is the hon. member quoting from and of what date is it?

I	am	quoting from Le
Soleil of October 13, 1925, from a report of its special correspondent bearing date Victoriaville, October 12. Now the Hon. J. E. Caron, Minister of Agriculture of that province, also took part in the campaign. He spoke at Levis at a meeting in the drill hall at which the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) was present, and in concluding his speech, as reported in L'Evenement of October 6 he said:

The Maritime Rights group-

Our province is situated in the gulf of St. Lawrence. It is 134 miles long and from 9 to 34 miles in width. I make this explanation because many of my friends ask me questions about Prince Edward Island. As I have suggested, a great many of the members have said nothing about the constituencies from which they come. How can we get acquainted with each other and know each other's problems if we do not learn something about the places from which other hon. members come? We are situated about nine miles from the mainland at the nearest point, and there is a car ferry operating between our province and the mainland all the year round. We have other means of getting away from the island in the summer time, but not in the winter. The car ferry is practically the only solution of our problem. We are very .grateful for that car ferry, because it is doing excellent work. Some days it will make only one trip, and some days several, depending on the amount of ice encountered on the trip. We are in a rather dangerous position down there, however, on account of the fact that we have just the one car ferry in operation. The ferry is a splendid one, in charge of a good captain and an efficient crew, but if anything happened to it we would be in great danger; I could hardly say what the effect might be upon the life of the community. A second car ferry is an imperative necessity in order to supplement the work done by the present one. I know that the hon. members who represent the different constituencies in this country would be willing to assist us and to see that we are protected in this way. We have a tourist business which gives us a good income down there. We have more and more tourists every year. I presume this is no place for advertising, but if any hon. members desire to spend a very pleasant holiday they cannot do better than come to Prince Edward Island, We will look after you in good shape. We have a tourist association which is doing good work, and it is officered by splendid men. We have also a disease-free area, and I believe that oan be said of only one or two other sections of Canada. The president of the Board of Trade spoke of this disease-free area as follows:

Now, Mr. Speaker, the question has been asked, what are Maritime rights? We hear a good deal about them. Maritime rights, boiled down, in essence are simply justice, fair play to all, equal rights and privileges such as should be given to all Canadian citizens, irrespective of colour, class or creed. In other words, Maritime rights are partnership rights, and we the people of Prince Edward Island expect we shall receive fair play as partners in the business of ruling this country. That is all we ask. We have our local difficulties, one of the chief of which is of course transportation, and in many respects a government favourably disposed to the province can help us. I have no doubt that when these difficulties are brought to the attention of the government in an adequate way they will be dealt with satisfactorily. But what we need above everything else, as I intimated before, is a second car ferry, and I emphasize this fact. It will take some time to get that car ferry in operation and the sooner its construction is taken in hand the better it will be for the province. I would therefore plead for special consideration in this regard.

Measures will be taken to further the retention on the land of our existing agricultural population, to encourage the return to rural parts of urban dwellers possessed of agricultural experience, and the repatriation of Canadians now living in other countries. But for another reason I find myself unable to vote for the amendment; the situation in regard to coal is one that calls for serious consideration. I Should like to help our friends in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick as far as possible, but I doubt very much whether I could favour a duty on coal, as we have no coal in our own province, and a duty would only mean an increase in price to the consumer. I think however that there should be a subsidy bearing equally on the shoulders of all. The amendment goes on to say:
-to enilarge the volume of employment in Canada and particularly to give to the producers of farm products, coal and other primary products the advantage they are, under present world conditions, entitled to enjoy in rtihe markets of this country.
I could not vote for such an amendment. Throughout the campaign we were told time and time again that we of this party were free traders, and I denied that suggestion; I said that we did not want to legislate exclusively in the interests of any class but that we wanted to use common sense. An hon. member the other night said that what we wanted was horse sense, and I think that is about right. I told my friends on the platform and in the press as well that if elected I would not have my hands tied in the matter of the tariff; I would not have a tariff that could not be changed but rather an adjustable schedule which, if it were too high in any direction, could; be sufficiently reduced, or which on the other hand could be increased where a reasonable increase might stimulate industry without injury to the interests of the country at large. The province from which I come is an agricultural country and it is necessary that, in whatever legislation its representatives support, the interests of the farmers should be consulted. For this reason I hope that the tariff board will be appointed, and

on that board I should think that there should be men representing all phases of activity in the Dominion who would make a study of tariff conditions and would be able to recommend just where a particular situation demanded an increase or where a reduction was necessary. If for example it were felt that the duty on eggs coming from the United States into Canada should be increased I would support any recommendation the board might make in that regard after it had1 had an opportunity to look into the situation thoroughly. I am not going to have my hands tied in the matter of the tariff but I shall use my best judgment as to what is best for the country. I believe that the tariff board would be one of the best institutions we could have in Canada. There is a tariff commission in the United States but it has not worked satisfactorily; it reports not to congress but direct to the president. Now I certainly would not favour a tariff board in his country with absolute control over the tariff and not responsible to parliament. I read the other day a significant statement in a New York paper, that certain manufacturers had appeared before the tariff commission with a request for an increase in the duty on certain manufactured articles. They already enjoyed a tariff of 75 per cent and they wanted an increase of 50 per cent. The commission recommended favourably to the president but he returned the recommendation with the comment that he would not allow the people to be bled any further by the manufacturers in this particular line. So that even in the United States they are beginning to realize that high protection is not always the panacea for all the ills which our friends opposite claim it to be.

The difficulty in our western provinces, as I understand it, Mr. Speaker, is largely due to the fact that we have the misfortune in Saskatchewan and in Alberta of having had Liberal governments for many long years. In fact the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan have never yet had an opportunity to know and to understand the real value of Conservative government. The prairie provinces were formed twenty-one years ago, and now that they have become of age I hope that they will exercise better judgment and be more careful in the guardianship of their great resources. I believe they are improving to some extent; but the improvement up to the present is not very marked; otherwise they would not be appealing to this parliament for assistance by way of rural credits. I wish to present a few examples of what I mean when I say that these provinces have suffered a great deal as a result of maladministration.
In 1917, just before the provincial election, the legislature of Alberta hurriedly passed certain legislation. First of all they passed an act entitled The Alberta Co-Operative Credit Act. Then they passed the Alberta Farm Loan Act; then the Live Stock Encouragement Act, and a fourth was the Seed Grain Act. I desire to point out the effect and purpose of the Alberta Co-Operative Act. This legislation provided for the formation of co-operative societies which might borrow money from the banks or any other source. It was intended to supply the needs of the farmers for short term loans. The municipalities within which the societies operate under this act may guarantee such loans up to one-half the subscribed capital, and the province may also give a guarantee up to one-half. The farmers generally have not availed themselves of the provisions of this act. I understand that the total amount borrowed by these societies in the whole province since 1917 amounts to about $935,000. The cost of the administration' of the act was borne entirely by the government of Alberta.

Let hon. gentlemen bear this in mind, that on November 4th, 1925, Senator Hale and Representative Hersey, both of Maine, pleaded with President Coolidge to remove the American duty upon Canadian potatoes. Would wTe not like to have that benefit? Sir, I have been in the Maritime provinces and I know that the farmers there would be proud to get access to the markets of the eastern states for the
greater part of their agricultural products. And what about our Canadian west? When I was in Minnesota about two or three weeks ago I found that Canadian potatoes were coming down by the carload, paying the American duty, and enjoying the market there at a fair margin of profit. What are the facts? I have the returns showing the shipment of .potatoes for the last three months. A return which came from the Bureau of Statistics to-day shows that for the three months of October, November and December, 1925, we shipped to the United States $2,436,591 worth of potatoes, paying fifty cents per hundredweight, and finding a market for those articles in that country. Would it not be of benefit to our western people to have free access or freer access into that great market for our cattle? We would then be in sight of the best market in the world. In Ontario, during the last four years, when we had free access for our cattle to the market, I was able to get, right on my own farm, within fifty cents per hundredweight of the highest quotations on the Chicago market. It would mean all the difference between success and failure in the live stock and fat cattle trade of Canada, and the live stock business is, as every farmer knows, the very right arm of a permanently successful agriculture. If hon. members of this House would give my right hon. friend the leader of the opposition the opportunity, he would begin at once to raise the tariff.
With such an object lesson right at our door, with the condition of unrest among the American farmers on account of high protection, why should our government not encourage trade between the two countries? They should not neglect this market. They should cultivate the friendship of the American people and try to obtain the benefits of that market. Is that trade between the two countries, in the face of the two tariff walls built up by each government against the products of the people, not at once a tribute to the power of natural trade laws and an indication of the only rational policy? Yet, in the face of those two tariff walls, for the last tw'elve months ending 31st October, 1925, over $1,020,000,000 of goods jumped over the two tariff walls back and forth between the two countries. That gives you an idea of what the people think, namely that trade is not a national matter. It is a matter between individuals. If a Canadian wants to buy anything across the border he does so for only one reason. He thinks he can get better value for his money there than any other place in the world. If an American

The Address-Mr. McMillan
does business here it is for the same reason. The citizens of the two countries think this international trade is so mutually beneficial that almost one-half of our entire foreign trade is conducted with the United States. These are not petty, partisan matters, but great problems of government which appeal for solution to the sense and judgment of every member of this House regardless of political* leanings. Therefore I solicit the support of all hon. members,-not as Liberals, not as Conservatives, not as Progressives or Independents, but as Canadian citizens, with the true interests of this country at heart-in order that together we may strengthen the hands of the present government so that they may carry to further fruition the policies they have put in operation.
A great deal hits been said respecting the Prime Minister, in his absence, which ought not to have been said. I have known the Right Hon. Mr. Mackenzie King for many years. There is no man in this House or out of it more scrupulously eager to uphold and preserve the high traditions of parliamentary practice; and, Sir, his course on this momentous occasion has been such that in years to come, when this generation shall have passed away, other men representing the Canadian people will recall with pride the most exemplary conduct of the Prime Minister of Canada on this occasion.
I can assure this House that in the hands of our brilliant leader Liberalism is not a decadent force in this country. Liberalism in his hands and through the medium of his policies, is a vital, living, active, progressive force in our political life, and a force which is always striving to make the achievements of to-day simply the base of operations for the progress and advancement of to-morrow. Away ^ with this little petty partisan spirit of Gritism or Toryism, or any other "ism," which can never look past its own doorstep but is always wondering what will give us this sectional advantage, or that personal or party favour, regardless of the true interests of the country. Away with such a spirit. If we as members of this House look upon ourselves merely as the creatures of a day, then, Sir, it makes little difference what we do, or whether we rob and despoil this rich heritage which we possess. On the other hand if we as true representatives of the people will look upon humanity as a seif-perpetuating race and upon ourselves as trustees for those who come after us, endeavouring to maintain the present good conditions and to make them even better, that those who Come after us may have a 
fairer dwelling place and more congenial living conditions than we enjoy-if that is our spirit then it is our duty to strengthen the hands of the brilliant leader of this government who in the space of one parliament has demonstrated his capacity most efficiently to represent Canada both at home and abroad, and W'hose government has already shown its ability to correct abuses, check monopoly, restore efficiency, reduce expenditures, lighten our tax burden, open up new and favourable markets, foster trade, and withal encourage and build up a spirit of unity and co-operation among all sections of this country and among all classes of our Canadian people.

In rising to offer a few observations on the subject matter before the House, I purpose at least to be brief and to keep as closely as possible to the point. But before referring to this subject matter, may I make some comments upon the attitude of a portion of the press, upon the editorial attitude in particular. We in this House know, and the country knows, that we have gone through during the past few days, a very difficult situation arising out of the peculiar complexion of the House, and during that time it has been natural, it has been inevitable, that much discussion should take place. I for one as a member of this House resent the imputation that all public men and all parties are rotten and corrupt. I take this view, that in thus attempting to impress the people of the country with the idea that parliament as an institution is not worthy of respect and that public men must of necessity be actuated by sordid and base motives, they have gone far, if these imputations are accepted by the people, not only to undermine confidence in public men but to forfeit the respect of the people for all law. For once people in this country are of the opinion that men on all sides of the House, that all political parties, that all public men are evil and corrupt, and that laws are passed under such an influence, what respect can there be for law and order? And if following that there comes an orgy of law-breaking, a carnival of crime, then I say that amongst those responsible will be the editorial writers who have fostered such an impression. Speaking for myself, I must confess that when I came into this House four years ago I came with a low opinion of politics; I am afraid that the people who sent me here had rather formed that opinion too. But I am happy to say that during my service here in the past parliament, having had an opportunity of becoming personally acquainted with gentlemen on all sides, I have found that the average standard

The Address-Mr. Speakman
of morality is high among all parties in the House and that members of parliament have usually endeavoured to do the right thing. And I have verified my view in this respect.
We find in the Speech from the Throne a number of things that are undoubtedly beneficial, things that not only meet with the approval of western people but which have been endorsed by every member in this House. As a passing thought I may observe that I was pleased to hear the leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) make the statement the other day that in his opinion principles were greater than parties and policies than leaders. I heartily endorse that statement; and if such be the case and we glance over the Speech from the Throne, then I say, Mr. Speaker, that in spite of our depleted numbers it is evident that in the legislative policies of the government the principles of the Progressive force are coming to the front.
I shall pass over the somewhat vague expressions which are usually incorporated in the Speech from the Throne, for the purpose, I was almost going to say, of cluttering it up. There is for instance the customary reference to the prosperous state of the country. I believe the country is getting more prosperous but I have found that same expression in all Speeches from the Throne. And the intimation that this prosperity has been brought about largely through governmental action we can, I think, safely pass over. Then there is the somewhat vague talk about rural life being encouraged and conditions in the country being improved. That is a very fine sentiment no doubt, but after all it is not sentiments expressed in the Speech from the Throne that will improve conditions but the embodiment of those sentiments in adequate legislation. And until that adequate legislation comes before the House, is discussed, and is passed, the Speech from the Throne is merely an indication of intention and nothing more.
The first item in the Speech, which is of some interest to us from Alberta particularly, has reference to the transfer of the natural resources to that province. Naturally as an Albertan I rejoice that the long period of contention in this regard is at last being brought to a close. I understand that the agreement is one that is satisfactory to both governments concerned, and if that is the case it will certainly meet with my approval. I will say nothing further about that because we can judge of the agreement only when we see it.
Next we come to what in my opinion is one of the most vital pieces of suggested
legislation of which we can at present conceive, namely, the subject of rural credits.
I do not propose to discuss that question in detail at all. In my opinion the proper time to discuss such matters at length is when the actual legislation is before us. May I say, and say it very frankly, that we have had suggestions as to rural credits before but these suggestions have failed to become embodied in the form of practical legislation. So to speak, they have just remained astral bodies and no more. For four years the Progressives in this House have endeavoured to impress the government with the necessity for such a measure. In that endeavour they found sympathetic assistance from some few members on both sides, notably-and I am glad to say this-from the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) on this side. And we appreciate all the assistance given. But we have found also that in our effort to get something done we have met with apathy from the major portion of both parties, and with active hostility on the part of some on either side. Now there is a change, and that which was formerly a forlorn hope has become if not a reality at least a principle that is accepted by everyone. I think that Canada ought to be congratulated on that result.
I listened with some interest when the hon. member for South Winnipeg (Mr. Rogers) made his references to this subject. I was unable to follow him in the entirety of his speech as I sit at some distance from him, but I seemed to gather from his remarks that the need for rural credits in Alberta and Saskatchewan was due solely to the fact that Conservative governments were not in power there, while in Manitoba, where a greater degree of good sense had been shown by the people, the need was not so pressing. I wondered if that could be the case and I recalled two facts out of past history. In the first place the need for rural credits was not so much the result of provincial activity or inactivity as it was the result of certain federal policies. It came as the result of a pronounced determination on the part of the government of that time, a determination with which I can find no fault, to encourage the output of farm products to the limit. It was impressed upon every farmer throughout the west that his patriotic duty demanded that he produce and produce to the uttermost, and as a result of the impetus thus given and the high prices then prevailing every farmer who was in a position to do so extended his production to the limit. And because of that extended activity the farmer

The Address-Mr. Speakman
became financially embarrassed. Now we have the aftermath. I wish to call the attention of hon. members to the fact that it was not under the regime of a Liberal government in Ottawa that this matter first came to the front. I am not saying that it was because of Conservative policies in the capital that we needed rural credit; nor am I suggesting that it was because of Liberal policies carried out in Alberta and Saskatchewan. It was simply due to the fact that every business in the country required then, as it requires now, financing along proper lines suitable to its particular activities. However, I will reserve the discussion of the actual legislation until the actual legislation is submitted to us, when I shall pronounce upon it.
The next point is one which is of interest chiefly to the provinces of Manitoba and Saskatchewan; I refer to the Hudson Bay railway. I am not going to discuss this question inasmuch as it is not a matter of vital interest to all the people of Alberta. We support it not because it will bring direct benefits to ourselves but because it is fair and just to the nation. Time was when we looked in that direction for relief, but things have changed and our eyes are now turning westward. To us the development of the western port of Vancouver and the framing of proper freight regulations governing that traffic are of infinitely greater importance. But for that reason, are we to take the view that a project which appealed to us as sound at one time when we felt the need of it ceases to be sound when we as individuals no longer require it? That would be the acme of selfishness, and we are therefore supporting it to the utmost. We do not know, and I am not persuaded, that the ocean route is feasible. I have remained in the House session after session when this matter was under discussion. I have found apparently expert opinion stating with authority and emphasis that the ocean route was absolutely feasible anywhere from five to nine months in the year. On the other side, I have found opinion, speaking with equal authority, to the effect that the route could never be so utilized. I do not know which opinion to accept. But this I do know, that under present conditions', in view of the large expenditure that has already been made, it is proper to complete the laying of steel and so open up what we believe to be a fine mineralized country in the Hudson bay territory. Having placed ourselves in that position, we can trust to future traffic to show whether the ocean route itself is feasible. That is the only way in my opinion in which the feasibility or otherwise of that route can be demonstrated. To that extent and! with

those motives, I can assure the House that we from Alberta are prepared to stand side by side with our brother members from the other provinces in seeking completion of the Hudson Bay railway.
But may I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that there is another transportation problem which has not been mentioned in the Speech from the Throne? We in Alberta not only have our transportation problem as a provincial problem but as part of a great national problem. I refer to the opening up of that vast empire to the north-the Peace river country. We strongly hope that this matter will yet be given most serious and earnest consideration in all parts of the House. I shall leave it to the hon. member representing that district, who understands the conditions far better than I do and can speak with much greater authority, to deal with that problem, merely adding that I wish the House to bear in mind that we have not forgotten it.
It is proposed to appoint a royal commission to investigate what are commonly known as Maritime rights. I do not know the Maritime provinces very well. I am a Nova Scotian only by marriage, but my dearest possession having come from that province, I have taken a very deep interest in Maritime affairs ever since, and I have grasped every opportunity to study questions affecting the Maritime provinces because I realize that a cancer spot in any part of this country is a source of weakness to the body politic as a whole. I do not know exactly what is needed. I do appreciate, however, that there are perhaps no two parts of Canada whose interests are more comparable than those of my native province of Alberta and of the Maritime provinces. I know that our problems are largely similar. We have a great coal area, and our difficulty is to convey the coal to the central markets of Canada. I understand that transportation is also one of the great problems of the Maritime provinces. Together they form a national problem of major importance, and I believe that by honest co-operation in the study of this and other problems affecting the east and the west we shall be able to settle upon a policy which will be beneficial to both. In this way we shall be rendering a great national service.
I am anxious to discuss with the representatives from the Maritime provinces their peculiar problems.
Speaking of coal, two suggestions have been made: One, to place a tariff on coal; the other, a low freight rate. Now, as to a tariff upon coal I am not so sure. I am a free trader, it is true, but I am a common sense trader, and I Should like to apply free trade principles

The Address-Mr. Speakman
in a common sense manner. However, I am dubious of the value of a tariff on coal, for two reasons. In the first place, our climatic conditions necessitate large quantities of fuel every winter, and I doubt the soundness of any policy which might materially increase the cost of fuel to our people. Secondly, I doubt the efficacy of such a method. We who have studied the industrial life of this country know that in many parts we are just on the dividing line as to the source of motive power. Electricity is more and more coming into use, and displacing coal, oil also is being more generally used in many places, and I fear that any policy which would materially increase the cost of fuel for power purposes would tend to still further contract the market for coal in favour of other sources of power. I am not taking a dogmatic view, but I appreciate the danger and difficulty of following such a course. I also appreciate that transportation is another great problem-the ability to carry coal or any other product from the far-flung portions of this Dominion to the great markets in the central provinces.
Now, what policy can be evolved that will best meet the situation? First, we must have a basis of .policy, that is, we must have knowledge. We have reached the conclusion, and we believe it is sound, that the first step to be taken before a satisfactory coal policy can be established is to ascertain beyond doubt what is the actual cost of transportation. We endeavoured to do that two years ago when a measure passed this House placing certain sums of money at the disposal of the government to recoup the National Railways for any loss it might incur by transporting coal from Alberta to Ontario at a cost of $7 a ton. The railway was to keep cost accounts and to be reimbursed the difference between that rate and the actual cost of transportation. On account of strikes in the Alberta coal field at that time the experiment was not made. Next session a sum of money was voted by the Dominion House and also by the legislature of Alberta with the same object in view, the granting of a flat rate of $7 per ton, the railway to keep accurate cost accounts and to be reimbursed any loss on operation that such accounts might show. But unfortunately Sir Henry Thornton, as head of the National Railways, preferred to carry the coal at a flat rate of 17 a ton rather than incur the expense of keeping strict cost accounts. In order to solve the problem, I believe that the first step this House should take should be to insist on an examination by competent persons, independently of the
railway officials, of transportation costs. With the information which would thus be available we would know whether it is economically possible to transport coal from Alberta and the Maritimes to the central provinces at a rate that will make the business commercially practicable, and we shall be able to take whatever steps may be necessary to put into effect a sound policy. I am prepared to work with any man or any body of men in this House to obtain that knowledge and bring about such a policy.
There are a number of other items which I do not intend to discuss at any length. The hour is late and I wish to come to a somewhat important part-or what is now suggested to be a part-of the Speech from the Throne, the amendment before the House. I believe it is unnecessary to discuss further the legislation embodied in the Speech from the Throne -and why? Because it has been proposed by the government, endorsed by the leader of the opposition, approved by the Progressives, accepted by the Labour group, already passed upon and approved by the Senate, and apparently no one has any difference of opinion. Therefore why discuss it? But the amendment itself might possibly be more controversial. In effect, what does the amendment say? It calls upon us to express by our votes regret that the Speech from the Throne does not give any indication of policy designed to enlarge the volume of employment in Canada, and particularly to give to the producers of farm products, coal and other primary products, the advantage they are, under present world conditions, entitled to enjoy in the markets of this country. I have heard this amendment described as an adroit work. Possibly that is so. I believe the mover of the amendment capable of working anything adroitly, but knowing the right hon. gentleman, I believe he has the courage and the honesty of his convictions and that never, of set purpose, would he so word an amendment as to give the impression that it means anything different from what it does mean. I shall give my interpretation as I see it. I am sorry the right hon. gentleman is not in the House, because I should have asked him to correct me if my interpretation is inaccurate. I interpret it in this way; that we are called upon to express regret that the principle of protection has not been more adequately maintained and extended in the Speech from the Throne, particularly as applied to those products mentioned. I think there is no doubt as to the meaning. As the right hon. gentleman is not here, either by silence to give consent or to correct me if I am inaccurate, I can only proceed on that a*-

The Address-Mr. Speakman
sumption. But I am working on that assumption, basing it not only on the amendment itself, but upon the known and pronounced policies of the Conservative party, to which the right hon. gentleman has the firm and unwavering allegiance of his entire party. I think I can proceed safely upon that assumption with very little danger of being mistaken, and upon that assumption I shall express my opinion. Those who have been in this House for the past four years, as my colleagues on this side of the House, have no doubt as to my opinions on this matter. I may have been mistaken in my opinions; I claim no infallibility, but at least I believe that I have expressed those opinions so clearly, so unmistakably and so consistently that no one here having heard me before can have any doubt as to where I stand. I do not propose to express regret that the protective policy has not been further extended and expanded in the Speech from the Throne. For three years I have opposed the budget introduced by the party now sitting opposite in the throne of power because that budget, in my opinion, did not carry out the tariff principles of that party and did not meet with the approval of low tariff men. No one can say that there is any doubt as to my position, and in view of that position there is only one attitude which I may consistently take. I do not believe, Mr. Speaker, that it would be a wise or sound policy, even as regards the products of the farms, the coal and other primary products, to enhance the duty to any height. And why? As I have indicated, this is a country where the climatic conditions force upon us the necessity of abundant food, abundant fuel and warm clothing, and these necessities should be purchased as cheaply as possble. As a farmer representing farmers, I say that I would not wish to impose upon the consumers of this country as a whole greatly enhanced prices, even though they might partly redound to my own profit. It is not sound from a national point of view. So that holding these opinions and basing them as I do upon my interpretation of this amendment, I shall certainly oppose it.
Now, Mr. Speaker, what else can we say? We can say this. I have referred to the unfair attitude of the press regarding one aspect of affairs here, but I am going to refer to a very fair opinion as it is directed towards another aspect. As I have indicated', every member of this House is apparently in favour of certain legislation embodied in the Speech from the Throne. We present this ludicrous spectacle to gods and men, that believing those things sound, we cannot get together to 
put them in the form of legislation. If ever the people of this country-and some of whom have had grave cause to doubt the efficiency of the party system-need an object lesson on the fallacies into which the party system may lead men, it will be found here, when men will not get together to do what all agree should be done. Co-operation is a wonderful word, a word which has been sometimes done to death, but I really believe there is room for some cooperation here. The Olympian deities might well laugh at human faults and frailties when they find 244 men and one lady all agreed as to what should be done, and incapable of getting together long enough to do it.
We have talked of co-operation, and may I say this:	Some of those people who affect
at least to disparage that word have failed to grasp the significance of what is happening in Canada to-day, the significance of the greatest co-operative movement which ever took place in this world, the co-operative marketing movement in western Canada. They have failed to grasp what that means. And what does it mean? It means that men have learned, through bitter experience, that in order to succeed they must sacrifice some of their own personal rights and opinions and work together. Because of that another force has come into play which will have a direct and powerful influence upon the political life of this country. For many years we have not studied international relationships as they should have been studied, and market condition as they affect world trade. But when farmers themselves get together and by their own agents sell their own goods in the markets of the world, the study of these conditions is forced upon them. Through that co-operative marketing is coming into existence a tremendous force of public opinion which will find its reflex in our political life. Side by side, commercially and politically, the movement will go on-in separate organizations, it is true but all working towards the same end.
I am speaking of this for one moment, late though it is, because it appears to me as the greatest and most significant phase of public life in this country to-day. We formed the pools for two objects: first, to bring about a parity of exchange values with our products and those of other producers in this country, and secondly, to bring together producer and consumer and eliminate the barriers which separated them. Forced by the nature of our commodity into world trade, what did we find? We found that tariffs were among those barriers, and the very reasons which led us to form these pools will lead us to fight

Alberta Coal
against trade restrictions. The two work together hand in hand, embody the same spirit, are different expressions of the same ideal, and although Progressive members may come and go and political bodies disappear, that co-operative movement will go on and that ideal will grow. In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, the time will come when, not only in western Canada but in eastern Canada, that co-operative movement in commerce, yes and in politics, will dominate this country.
Some people think, and I have heard them say, that some of the members in this corner of the House are impossible idealists. Well,
